fixes.explanation: I wish it went that way, friend, but the text doesn't say that. It says Pashhur had Jeremiah beaten and put in the stocks (Jeremiah 20:2). Nothing in the verse mentions a request for prayer. A chief official who hears a warning and reaches for the stocks is a hard scene to picture, I think.

A meeting with the elders sounds so civilized, doesn't it? But the text says Pashhur had Jeremiah beaten and put in the stocks at the Upper Gate of Benjamin (Jeremiah 20:2). The elders don't come up in these verses. I think that tells us how he took the message.

Yes, baker! When Pashhur releases Jeremiah from the stocks, Jeremiah says to him, "The LORD does not call you Pashhur, but Magor-missabib." (Jeremiah 20:3). That's a prophet who still has the LORD's word to deliver.

Thank-you note? Nope, friend. The text doesn't record Jeremiah thanking Pashhur. He tells him, "The LORD does not call you Pashhur, but Magor-missabib." (Jeremiah 20:3). I think that's a very different kind of goodbye.

Nice try, but being in the stocks didn't stop Jeremiah from speaking. He speaks right to Pashhur and says, "The LORD does not call you Pashhur, but Magor-missabib." (Jeremiah 20:3). The text records no promise to stop. He keeps going.

Close in spirit, baker, but that's not the word. The LORD says, "I will make you a terror to yourself and to all your friends." (Jeremiah 20:4). A warning is something you hear, but the LORD says Pashhur himself will be a terror, to himself and to his friends. It's heavy, so take it slow.

Babylon is right, baker. The LORD says, "…I will hand Judah over to the king of Babylon…" (Jeremiah 20:4). That reaches past one man in the stocks, since it's all of Judah being handed over. The message was never just about Pashhur.

Egypt is a good guess, friend, but the LORD names a different king. He says He will hand Judah over to the king of Babylon, and that king will carry them away to Babylon (Jeremiah 20:4). Babylon is the word that goes in the blank.
Assyria is a good guess, friend, but it's not the word here. The LORD says, "…I will hand Judah over to the king of Babylon…" (Jeremiah 20:4). Babylon is the word that goes in the blank.

Hiding the treasure is a clever plan, friend, but it's not the one the LORD gives. He says He will give the wealth of the city to their enemies, who will plunder it and carry it off to Babylon (Jeremiah 20:5). The wealth gets carried away, not buried under the temple.

Right, baker. The LORD says, "You will go to Babylon, and there you will die and be buried…" (Jeremiah 20:6). It's a sober ending, and the text doesn't soften it. Pashhur goes to Babylon, and there he dies and is buried.

I'd love a happy homecoming, friend, but that's not what the LORD says. He says, "You will go to Babylon, and there you will die and be buried…" (Jeremiah 20:6). His words end with Pashhur dying and being buried in Babylon, and they mention no escape or trip home. It's a sad line.

False is right, baker. The LORD says Pashhur's friends are the ones "…to whom you have prophesied these lies." (Jeremiah 20:6). So what Pashhur prophesied to them was lies, not the truth. I think that makes the stocks sit even heavier.
